Market Desk · Daily Debrief · Monday, November 23, 2026

Nvidia got its CEO back and the market had its best day since April 2025. The trend didn't change.

The S&P 500 rose 4.7% to 7,237, the Nasdaq 6.5%, and Nvidia 31.5% after its board reinstated Jensen Huang. But the index stopped at the first real ceiling, the 2-year yield went up, and the Fed is still pricing a hike on Dec 9. Our read: a violent short-covering rally inside a downtrend, not a new uptrend. Here is why, and what we do with it.

The miss first. The PLTR Dec 18 $150 put idea sat 1.9% from its first target on Friday's close and gave nearly all of it back today: the paper mark went from $1,390 to $595 as PLTR jumped 11.1%. Holding it near the target was a bad trade on Friday already (more in the lesson). Two put ideas also broke before they ever triggered: INTC (+16.3%) closed over its 14-day, which was the thesis-broken line, and GOOGL gapped through its $276 out line. Both are cancelled. The JPM put idea did trigger intraday, and it held: JPM closed $316.66, under the $319 line.

What mattered today
  • Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO (8-K, unanimous board vote). NVDA +31.5% to $165.05 on 779M shares, 2.7x its 20-day average volume. No word on the SEC accounting review or the 10-Q, due Dec 4.
  • Best day for the S&P 500 since Apr 9, 2025: SPX +4.73% to 7,237.17, Nasdaq +6.51%, the Dow +3.01% (+1,448 points). SPX traded 7,295.60 and closed back under its 38.2% cluster (7,250–7,261).
  • Fear came out fast: VIX 35.89 → 26.62. Nomura's McElligott called it a "massive surge of MECHANICAL buying" (short covering and dealer hedges).
  • The Fed didn't move: NY Fed's Williams: "There is still work to do." Dec 9 hike odds about 91–93%. The 2-year rose about 6–9bp; the dollar index hit its highest since March 2025.
  • Oil fell 4.5%: WTI $80.17, Brent $89.37, after Trump said he'd give Iran diplomacy more time. Energy was the only S&P sector down.
  • Data: November flash services PMI 54.7 vs 55.6 expected (prior 56.1), prices easing. Dell reports tomorrow after the close; PCE and GDP come Wednesday.

  • BAC Dec 18 $47 put: ready on trigger, 1.0% away. A 15-minute close under $47.65 (today's low) breaks the bounce; stop a 15-minute close over $48.60; target the 52-week low $45.64. R:R 2.1 to 1 (option 2.6). $104 a contract, FAIR. Lines up with force 3.

The combination is the story. Stocks had their best day in 19 months, yet the 2-year yield rose and the dollar made a 20-month high. The bond market did not buy the idea that the Fed can relax; it priced the same December hike it priced on Friday. Oil fell on the Iran headline, which takes some pressure off inflation later, but not by Dec 9. Gold bounced 3% after a 9% weekly drop, a relief move more than a new trend. For our names: rising short rates with a flat 10-year squeeze bank margins (JPM, BAC), and a firm dollar plus a hiking Fed caps how far the AI rebound can run before the data catch up with it.

What's going on

Four forces behind the day

1. Nvidia's governance scare ended. The accounting question didn't.

What we see: NVDA +31.5% to $165.05, adding close to $1 trillion of market value. The chip ETF SMH rose 15.0%, Micron 19%, CRDO 22.6%, DELL 20.5%, BE 18.1%, INTC 16.3%.

Why: Nvidia's 8-K says the board voted unanimously to reinstate Huang after it "received input from senior levels of the United States government" and is confident he "poses no national security risk." Kress goes back to CFO. A board committee will finish its probe, and Nvidia is adding a National Security and Export Control Committee and a Chief Compliance Officer. Analysts moved fast: Bernstein upgraded to Outperform ($200 target), Citi raised to $240, Goldman kept Buy at $220 but called the investigations "an overhang."

What the 8-K does not say: anything about the SEC staff review Reuters reported on Nov 20, or the 10-Q that is due by Dec 4. Three House committees interview Huang on Dec 1 about chip diversion to China. Today removed the leadership risk; the filing risk is still on the calendar.

What would prove us wrong: a clean 10-Q filed early with no restatement. That would take away the last reason AI hardware traded at a discount, and the chip bounce could become a trend. Names: NVDA, SMH, AMD, INTC, CRDO, DELL, BE, VRT; PLTR and ORCL by sympathy.

2. A short squeeze, not yet a new uptrend

What we see: the S&P 500 rose 4.7% but the equal-weight version (RSP) only 2.6%, so the biggest stocks did the heavy lifting. Midday, advancers led decliners about 4.4 to 1 on the NYSE, yet the Nasdaq still printed 207 new lows against 15 new highs. QQQ's opening jump was the biggest since it launched in 1999.

Why: Nomura's Charlie McElligott called it a "massive surge of MECHANICAL buying": funds covering shorts and dealers unwinding the put hedges they had bought last week, and he said the bounce "guarantees us nothing." Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson went the other way and called last week's drop an overshoot, "a buying opportunity too good to miss." Goldman's desk was constructive but warned the capitulation a lasting bottom usually needs may be missing.

Our read: the chart sides with McElligott for now. SPX tagged 7,295.60, over the 38.2% of the Mar 30 → Oct 6 run (7,260.97) and the 38.2% of the Oct 6 → Nov 20 drop (7,250.09), and closed under both. It is still under its 14-day (7,405), 30-day (7,553) and 200-day (7,350). What would change our mind: SPX closing over 7,364 (the 200-day plus the 50% of the drop). Then calls come back on the table. Names: everything, but most of all the call ideas we are not taking.

3. The Fed is still hiking, and the bond market agreed today

What we see: the 2-year rose roughly 6–9bp to about 4.70% while the 10-year barely moved, so the curve flattened. The dollar index rose 0.5% to about 104.3, its highest since March 2025. December hike odds held near 91–93% (CME FedWatch).

Why: New York Fed President John Williams, the last scheduled speaker before the blackout, said "We must take actions over time that will ensure that we get inflation back to our 2% goal… There is still work to do." He sees inflation back at 2% only in 2028. On Friday Governor Cook said waiting longer "risks getting behind the curve." The flash PMI was softer (services 54.7 vs 55.6 expected) with prices paid easing, but not enough to change December.

What it means for the ideas: a hiking Fed with a flat curve is the case behind the JPM $305 put and the new BAC $47 put: short-term funding costs rise faster than what banks earn on long loans. The firm 2-year also caps the rebound in long-duration tech, which supports the GOOGL $270 put and the AMZN $240 put idea. The PLTR $150 put needs PLTR back under its 200-day ($154.09) to work again. What would prove us wrong: a soft core PCE on Wednesday (consensus +0.3% m/m) that knocks hike odds under 70%.

4. Oil gave up the war premium

What we see: WTI settled $80.17 (−4.5%), its first settle near $80 since August; Brent $89.37 (−3.5%), down about a fifth in November. XOM −1.9%, OXY −2.2% to a new low for the move, while DAL rose 5.4%.

Why: President Trump said he would "give Iran diplomacy more time," so traders unwound weekend hedges. Gulf barrels are still flowing despite the tanker attacks near Hormuz, and the IEA sees a surplus of about 2 million barrels a day this quarter. We could not confirm the reported Nov 29 OPEC+ meeting in today's sources.

What it means: the OXY $55 put idea is working (OXY $52.70, $4.91 above its first target), and the XOM put we considered fails our 2-to-1 rule (see the skip box). What would prove us wrong: talks collapse and the tanker attacks escalate; oil would gap up and both energy names with it.

Top: NVDA +31.5%, CRDO +22.6%, DELL +20.5%, BE +18.1%, INTC +16.3%, SMH +15.0%. Down: OXY −2.2%, XOM −1.9%, ANT −1.4%, KO −1.1%, XLE −1.1%.

Read the chart right to left: the names that fell hardest last week (NVDA, CRDO, DELL, BE, INTC) bounced hardest today. Only oil and staples fell. That is what short covering looks like.

The market, in one picture

SPX failed at the first ceiling

Key levels: 7,364 (200-day 7,350 + 50% of drop) · 7,250–7,261 (38.2% cluster, rejected) · 7,081–7,110 (floor) · 6,900 (61.8%).

It rejected the 38.2% cluster at 7,250–7,261 after trading to 7,295.60, and it is still under the 14-day (7,405) and 30-day (7,553); the 14-day crossed under the 30-day on Oct 29, so direction is down. The 50-day (7,618) is still over the 200-day (7,350), so the bigger trend is up: this is a pullback in an uptrend that keeps getting deeper.

How we read it: Friday's low wicked under the 61.8% of the big run (6,900.46) and closed back over it; today held the floor at 7,081–7,110 (50% of the big run and 23.6% of the drop). The next close decides: over 7,364 (200-day + 50% of the drop) and the squeeze has legs; back under 7,081 and today was a one-day event. Until then no new calls: the S&P's own 14/30 says down.

Lesson of the day

Why the PLTR put lost 57% on an 11% move

Holding a play near its target is a new trade, and it is usually a bad one. On Friday PLTR closed $143.49. The put idea's first target was $140.71, just $2.78 away. Its exit was a close over $166.09, $22.60 away. Holding from Friday's close was a bet paying $2.78 against a risk of $22.60: 0.12 to 1. We would never open that trade, yet holding it was the same decision.

What it cost: PLTR rose $15.87 today and the $150 put fell from $13.90 to $5.95, −57% on an 11% move. Three things did that. Delta: the put moved about 42 cents per dollar on average, starting near 0.5 and shrinking to 0.32 as PLTR rose (that shrinking is gamma), about $6.70 of the loss. Volatility: implied volatility fell from 66.8% to 62.4%, and with vega near 0.15 that is about $0.66. Time: three calendar days of theta at about $0.19 a day, about $0.57.

The rule we take from it: when a close leaves a play within about 1 ATR of target 1 (PLTR's ATR is $10.16; it was 0.3 ATR away), the play is TOO LATE for anyone new and the paper record takes the profit at the next intraday read, unless a fresh R:R from that price passes 1.5 to 1 to target 2. Logged for the Friday review as a proposed rule.

Fib in action

NVDA: the daily says wick, the 2-day says reclaim

Key levels: 2-day close $165.05 · 0.786 ext $170.22 (lesson) · 0.5 ext $155.33 · 1.382 ext $201.24.

NVDA: two timeframes, one level (concept 17). The desk's NVDA extension is drawn on 2-day candles: A $164.61 (Mar 13), B $216.66 (Apr 21), C $129.31 (Oct 30, 2025), so B − A = $52.05. The 0.786 = 129.31 + 0.786 × 52.05 = $170.22; the 0.5 = 129.31 + 0.5 × 52.05 = $155.33.

What price did: on the daily chart NVDA's high ($171.50) went $1.28 over the 0.786 and closed under it ($165.05). That looks like a failure. But the drawing lives on the 2-day chart, and the 2-day candle (Nov 20–23) ran from $124.50 to $171.50 and closed $165.05: back over the 0.5 it lost on Nov 18, still under the 0.786. On its own timeframe the 0.5 was reclaimed and the 0.786 was not tested on a close at all.

Which one wins: the timeframe the level was drawn on decides held or broke; the shorter chart only times the entry. So: no put while the 2-day closes over $155.33, and a call needs a 2-day close over $170.22 plus the 14-day turning up (it would also need the S&P to allow calls). The trade, when it comes, aims at the next level: the 30-day ($191.80) and the 1.382 ($201.24), with the stop under the level just reclaimed.

Check it on the chart: how far apart are the 1.382 ($201.24) and the 30-day ($191.80)? About 4.9%: two separate stall zones, not one cluster.
